components.text: The decisive demand is whether failure of physical emergence selects idealism while preserving an explained objective order.
The parsimony move must justify why epistemic givenness establishes a uniquely mental ontology.
The decisive demand is whether rejecting physical emergence makes idealism preferable over other nonmaterialist accounts.
The decisive demand is to show how idealism can retain an observer-independent, structured external world.
The decisive demand is for idealism to preserve an observer-independent, structured external world rather than merely relabel experience.
The decisive demand is whether labeling the inaccessible external substrate mental explains representation, machinery, and boundaries.
The decisive demand is whether labeling the inaccessible represented substrate mental explains the machinery and origins of predictive representation.
The decisive demand is to account for boundaries, biological differentiation, and stable predictive order under idealism.
The decisive demand is for an account of representational boundaries, biological differentiation, and stable natural organization under idealism.
The earlier objection also demands an account of the world's observed structure and order rather than a dissociation label alone.
The decisive demand is to avoid the hard problem without presuming a physical object that generates experience.
The foundational inference must exclude a neutral representational basis rather than only nonexperiential matter.
The decisive demand is whether a nonmaterialist alternative can avoid the hard problem while accommodating phenomenal character.
The opening move also requires a reason that consciousness, rather than a neutral representational basis, is the sole parsimonious foundation.
The decisive demand is whether representational or illusory self-models can possess phenomenality without presupposing consciousness.
The decisive inference is that dissolving the enduring personal self can remove the need for consciousness as the condition of experienced representations.
The decisive demand is to locate phenomenality after the organizing phenomenal self-model has dissolved.
The decisive demand is to explain phenomenality after distinguishing consciousness from the limited organizing self-model.
The decisive demand is whether integrated processes outside the narrative self can retain their own subjective viewpoints.
The decisive demand is whether excluded and non-narrative representational processes can possess their own subjective viewpoints.
The decisive demand is why greater integration or a maximal complex entails any subjective point of view.
The decisive demand is why integrated information entails phenomenality and what greater or lesser consciousness means.
The decisive demand is whether IIT provides more than correlation by grounding phenomenality in self-existing causal structure.
The decisive demand is whether IIT supplies more than an empirical mapping and what ontological conclusion its causal structure supports.
The decisive demand is to identify the self-existing subject that supposedly possesses causal power in the dream analogy.
The decisive demand is to identify the self-existing causal subject when the account says a dreamer causes an imagined object.
The earlier concession that personal selves are representational creates a tension with treating an ordinary first-person self as causal.
The decisive demand is to identify a causal subject without reinstating the unstable narrative personal self.
The decisive demand is to identify a causal bearer of experience that is not the unstable narrative personal self.
The decisive demand is to explain differentiated dream events when no experienced personal self directs or causes them.
The decisive demand is how a universal nonpersonal subject differentiates and causes one particular dream element rather than another.
The move also asks whether IIT identifies the particular causal factors operative in an ordinary selfless dream.
The decisive demand is to explain differentiated causal order without appeal to a directing personal self.
The decisive demand is how one universal subject yields differentiated events and complex causal order without a personal agent.
The decisive demand is whether the field account requires ordinary spatial and temporal organization to explain experience.
The decisive earlier demand would be whether excitation modes explain differentiated causal order in universal subjectivity.
The meditative case bears on whether experience and subjectivity require ordinary spatial or temporal organization.
